Question: What are the things you hate to experience when selling your house?
Old_Answer: You can't help feeling emotional about the home you have lived in and loved. You've lavished thought and money over the decor. It's part of you in a way. So when potential buyers come round and wrinkle their noses at it, it's not nice. That's why estate agents are useful. They know what to say to get the sale. they don't care about the colour you painted the walls in, and if a viewer says something disparaging, they know not to defend the choice but to say how easy it would be to paint over it. Whenever I've sold houses in the past I've always gone through it thoroughly with the agent but then left it to them.

First off, the seemingly endless stream of viewings by people who are just not serious can get under your skin. You tidy up, leave the house, and then they don’t even seem interested. Next up, there’s the dreaded feedback from potential buyers. The classic “it’s not you, it’s me” line is infuriating when you’ve put your heart and soul into making the place presentable, only for someone to find fault with your choice of paint color or the size of the garden. And let’s not forget the costs associated with selling; estate agent fees can feel like highway robbery, especially in a market that’s already tough. Then, there’s the waiting game; after accepting an offer, the drawn-out process of negotiations, surveys, and contracts can feel torturous. You think you’re close to the finish line, only to be thrown curveballs that can send the entire deal into a tailspin. Finally, there's the emotional toll; the house isn’t just bricks and mortar — it’s a home filled with memories. The thought of letting go can be haunting, and having to constantly remind yourself that this is a business transaction makes the whole process feel even colder. All in all, selling a house should be a happy occasion, but when you’re in the thick of it, it can feel like a test of endurance.

All of these elements combine to create a selling experience that is often fraught with tension and uncertainty, reminding us that real estate transactions are not just financial decisions but deeply personal journeys.

Question: What changes in British society and culture have been most striking over the past 70 years?
Old_Answer: I'm almost 70. When I was a kid in London, everyone smoked. Really everyone, including doctors. It was slightly unusual if an adult didn't. Now the reverse is true. No one picked up after their dog. You had to watch where you were walking. Everything is cleaner now. In the past, car ownership was very aspirational. I remember, as a car-mad youngster, ruthlessly judging adults on the car they drove. No one cares much now. National Service was expected. When the Conservatives floated the idea of bringing it back at the last election…well, let's just say it wasn't a vote winner. Murderers were still being hanged. No one (apart from a few extremists) wants that again. In fact people nowadays are much more likely to show understanding and pity when someone commits a crime. Children were labelled "stupid" for having what we now know are a wide range of learning disabilities. People were very deferential. If you look at old interviews of Harold Wilson by Robin Day, they were almost grovelling compared to the more provocative techniques used now. Parents didn't challenge their children's teachers. Now it's commonplace. People went to church. Now most of the population is atheist. People were not very socially mobile in the past. You stayed in your lane. We move up and down much more now. In the past, casual racism and sexism was normal. Now it's very much frowned upon. I don't remember liking my parents' taste in music much, but my kids like mine. I can't say they play the Beatles for instance, but the see merit in them. Seventy years ago, Britain was determined to export manufactured goods at all cost. It was very keen on doing business with Europe and wanted to cooperate with our closest neighbours and markets as much as possible. Now, sadly, Britain is more isolationist. Britain was a real world power, with the remnants of an empire and huge clout in the world. That's changed dramatically. In the 1950's it wasn't very common to see someone with dark skin. Now Britain is home to a huge range of cultures that all feed in to a very diverse mix.

Take, for example, the seismic shift in attitudes towards multiculturalism. Post-war Britain saw waves of immigration, particularly from the Commonwealth, which enriched the cultural tapestry but also sparked debates about identity and integration. Cities like London have become vibrant melting pots, featuring diverse cuisines, festivals, and languages. Moreover, the feminist movement has profoundly impacted gender roles, with women's rights gaining traction and leading to greater representation in politics, business, and media. The normalization of discussions around mental health and well-being marks another significant societal change, as the stigma has largely diminished, leading to more open conversations and support structures in place. Additionally, the advent of technology, particularly the internet and social media, has revolutionized communication, altering the way people connect, engage in politics, and consume media. This digital era has also prompted significant shifts in consumer behavior, reshaping industries from retail to entertainment. Finally, the ongoing discourse around climate change and sustainability has positioned environmental concerns at the forefront of public consciousness, influencing everything from policy-making to everyday choices. Together, these changes paint a picture of a society that is becoming increasingly complex, interconnected, and conscious of its past and future.

Question: How can one negotiate with their landlord to lower the rent? What factors should be considered when determining the percentage of reduction to ask for? How can this amount be calculated?
Old_Answer: Offer the landlord something in return, such as maintaining and cleaning the common parts. If there is a green area, offer to keep it tidy and cut. Offer to clean the windows regularly. Offer a longer tenancy agreement to save the landlord costs of renewing the TA after a year. You have to understand that landlords are running a business. Anything you can offer to lower their costs will be of interest. Calculate the benefit to them by asking a professional company to quote on doing the work, then offer to do it for less.
Answer_with_writing_sample: Negotiating with a landlord can feel daunting, but it’s essential to approach it with a clear strategy. First, assess your local rental market. If you notice similar properties in your area are renting for significantly less than what you currently pay, you have a strong basis for your request. Aim for a percentage reduction that feels reasonable; typically, asking for a decrease of 5% to 15% is often realistic, depending on how long you’ve been a tenant and your payment history. If you’ve been a reliable tenant—always paying on time and taking care of the property—highlight this as a bargaining chip. You might also want to consider the current economic climate; if the cost of living has risen or if your landlord has seen an increase in vacancies, this could work in your favor. When calculating the amount to request, consider your budget and how much you can realistically afford. For instance, if you currently pay £1,200 a month, a 10% reduction would amount to £120, bringing your rent down to £1,080. Prepare your case clearly and be ready to discuss your reasoning without becoming confrontational. It’s also helpful to suggest alternative solutions if a direct reduction isn’t possible, like waiving fees or extending the lease for a lower rate. Ultimately, remember that negotiation is about finding a mutually beneficial agreement, so be open to discussion and compromise.

Consider the current economic conditions, such as inflation rates and employment statistics, which may impact your landlord's willingness to negotiate. Respectful and well-prepared discussions often yield the best results, fostering a positive relationship that can benefit both parties in the long run.

Question: As a Korean descendant, I am boycotting Japanese products due to their cruelty to my ancestors. By that same logic, should Jews boycott German products due to the Nazis' actions?
Old_Answer: Possibly, but these events were a long time ago now and the perpetrators are all dead. Exactly who is benefitting from this boycott? Having said that, go ahead. It's your money. My mother didn't like the idea of owning a German car because she was an adult in wartime London and was bombed out. She wasn't Jewish, but just chose not to buy German stuff. In time her position softened and she even owned an Audi Coupé, but it was her choice.
Answer_with_writing_sample: Boycotting products based on historical injustices is a complex and deeply personal decision. As someone with Korean ancestry, I understand the sentiments that drive individuals to avoid products from nations associated with past atrocities. In the case of Japan, the legacy of colonialism and the suffering inflicted upon Koreans is a painful chapter that many carry with them. However, translating this logic to the Jewish experience with Germany is not as straightforward. The Holocaust represents an unspeakable horror, and the emotional and cultural ramifications are profound. While some may argue that boycotting German products is a form of protest against the historical atrocities committed by the Nazis, it is crucial to consider the current context. Many Germans today are not the perpetrators of those crimes, and the nation has made significant efforts to confront its past and promote reconciliation. For some, purchasing German products may even be seen as a form of support for a country that has transformed itself and recognizes its historical failings. Ultimately, the choice to boycott or not is deeply personal and varies among individuals within each community. It's a reflection not only of historical grievances but also of how we perceive accountability and healing in contemporary society. Thus, while some may feel justified in a boycott, others might see value in engaging with a nation that has evolved and takes steps to remember and learn from its past.

Question: Is it true that some doctors recommend smoking for health reasons? How much validity is there to this claim?
Old_Answer: What possible "health reason" legitimises a practice that kills millions every year?
Answer_with_writing_sample: There was a time when some doctors did indeed endorse smoking, albeit under the guise of certain health benefits. In the mid-20th century, a handful of physicians claimed that smoking could aid digestion or even reduce stress, which is ironic considering the vast body of evidence against such claims today. It was a period marked by a lack of understanding of the long-term health implications of tobacco use, and marketing campaigns cleverly exploited this naivety. For instance, tobacco companies would often feature doctors in their advertisements, endorsing specific brands as if they were the prescriptions of health professionals. Fast forward to today, and the narrative has dramatically shifted. The overwhelming consensus among modern medical professionals is that smoking is a leading cause of preventable diseases, including cancer, heart disease, and respiratory issues. To suggest that any health benefits from smoking hold validity is not only misleading but dangerous. We now understand the severe consequences of smoking, and public health initiatives continuously work to educate and reduce tobacco use. So, while it’s true that some doctors once recommended smoking, those claims lack any credibility in light of contemporary medical research. Smoking is unequivocally harmful, and any historical endorsement should be viewed through the lens of a bygone era of misinformation.

Claims of smoking being beneficial are not supported by credible scientific evidence. For anyone seeking to improve their health, embracing a smoke-free lifestyle is undoubtedly the most beneficial path, backed by substantial research and medical advice.

Question: Do adult immigrants forget their native language after living in another country for years and raising children there?
Old_Answer: My Dad left Austria when he was 8 in 1938 and lived the rest of his life in London. He spoke perfect English without an accent and avoided speaking his native language. In fact I can only remember hearing him speaking German to a few aged aunts who couldn’t speak English. All the rest of the time the Austrian side of my family all spoke English together even when they were not with an English member of the family (like my mother) who spoke no German. However my father and I spoke German to each other on a few occasions. I can’t remember why. I learned my German in Frankfurt in the 1970’s and 80’s, and noticed his Austrian accent and rather quaint turn of phrase. He spoke it quite perfectly though.
Answer_with_writing_sample: Immigrants can experience varying degrees of language retention depending on several factors, including the environment they live in, the language spoken at home, and the age at which they migrated. In my observations, many adults who move to a new country and raise children there often prioritize the dominant language of their new environment to ensure their kids are integrated and can communicate effectively. This can lead to a gradual loss of fluency in their native language, especially if they aren’t actively using it in their daily lives. I’ve seen this firsthand with friends who came from strong linguistic backgrounds; they initially maintained their native tongue at home, but as their children grew up, the shift toward the new language became evident. In contrast, immigrants who participate in community gatherings, cultural events, or maintain relationships with family back home often preserve their native language much better. It’s not uncommon for these individuals to switch between languages, a phenomenon known as code-switching, depending on their audience. But yes, for many, the native language may fade, leading them to feel less proficient over time. So while it’s entirely possible for adult immigrants to forget their native language, it’s not a guarantee; it largely depends on their commitment to maintaining it amidst the pressures of assimilation and the desire for their children to thrive in a new linguistic landscape.

Furthermore, bilingualism can actually enhance cognitive flexibility, allowing adults to navigate multiple languages effectively. In essence, while some may experience a degree of language attrition, many retain a significant connection to their native tongue, especially if they nurture that aspect of their identity. In conclusion, adult immigrants can experience varying degrees of language retention or loss, but the ability to forget a native language is not absolute and is influenced by individual circumstances and choices.
Answer_with_full_information: It's a common misconception that adult immigrants forget their native language entirely after years of residing in a new country, especially when raising children who may primarily speak the dominant language. While it’s true that language proficiency can diminish over time due to lack of use, the reality is far more nuanced. For many, their native language often remains a significant part of their identity and cultural heritage. Factors such as personal motivation, community engagement, and the presence of social networks in their native language play crucial roles in language retention. Moreover, children raised in bilingual environments have the potential to become fluent in both languages, which can serve as a bridge for their parents to maintain their native tongue. I’ve observed this phenomenon in many immigrant communities; parents often use their native language at home, which not only preserves the language but also reinforces cultural values and familial bonds. However, in cases where integration into the new culture is prioritized, or where the dominant language is overwhelmingly present in social and professional settings, some vocabulary or fluency may be lost. This doesn't equate to complete forgetfulness but rather a reshaping of language use, where bilingualism is more common than monolingualism in either language. Ultimately, the question hinges on individual circumstances, emphasizing that language is a fluid entity, shaped by social interactions and personal choices.

Question: How can one cope with negative experiences while traveling abroad? Is the effort of traveling worth it if it is not enjoyable?
Old_Answer: We've all had disappointments. The theft. The horrible meal. The rude shop assistant. The delayed flight. Not all were actually disasters though, so let's not over-dramatise things. The way I deal with it is to learn from the incident but to travel more. So because I had a horrible experience skiing in France, I still ski, but I go to Austria. I have kind of done Milan where I was ripped off so simply don't need to go there again…etc, etc. I focus on what I like and what has been successful, and do more of that, and I try not to repeat mistakes. But I try to keep it in perspective…one rude Parisian isn't going to ruin France for me. Later this year I'm driving a 1967 Mustang Fastback from London to Vienna. My route is going to take in places I love in France, Belgium, Germany, Switzerland and Austria, places I've always wanted to see, and I'm sure there will be one or two incidents that don't work out too well. That will be all part of the adventure.

So yes, while the occasional mishap might test your patience, it can also create stories that enhance your life long after the trip is over. Ultimately, it’s about appreciating the journey, including the bumps along the way, that makes travel worthwhile.

Old_Answer: I did, for quite a few years. I was working for an advertising agency (as a creative) by day and working on children's books as an illustrator by night. The agency didn't mind. Question: Were British people concerned about a potential German invasion during World War II? If so, what measures did they take to prepare for it?
Old_Answer: On the south coast of the U.K. there remain plenty of reminders of constructions designed to stall an invasion. I took this shot of "Dragons Teeth" near Poole recently. They are meant to stop tanks, or at least to channel them into killing fields. The south of England is littered with WW2 "pill box" machine gun nests. These brick and concrete bunkers were quickly erected all over the places where a landing by sea or air might conceivably occur. Beaches were guarded and mined. Cliffs were manned by lookouts and were covered in wire. So whilst no imminent invasion was ever expected, measures were taken. The public were concerned obviously, but my mother, born in London in 1920 said that she didn't ever lose sleep over it. My father, a child refugee from Vienna, did however.
